body.text: The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) is a non-refundable 3.5% credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures, claimed by corporations on Schedule T2SCH508 under Ontario's Taxation Act, 2007. It has no expenditure cap, can be carried back 3 years, carried forward 20 years or waived, and its base includes restored capital expenditures on or after December 16, 2024.

This report delivers a comprehensive technical audit and legal analysis of the research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture, statutory provisions, administrative policies, judicial precedents, provincial regimes, and direct innovation funding programs in Canada as of November 20261.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, Canada enacted the most significant structural expansion of its flagship Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program in over a decade2. Originating in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement tabled on December 16, 2024, expanded in the 2025 Federal Budget presented on November 4, 2025, by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne, and enacted into law upon the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, these reforms fundamentally alter Canadian R&D tax planning for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 20242. Key enacted measures include doubling the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual refundable federal credit on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000), broadening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a $15,000,000–$75,000,000 three-year average gross revenue phase-out (which Canadian-controlled private corporations may also elect to use), restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (including Shared-Use Equipment), and launching an optional CRA Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 20261.

Simultaneously, provincial R&D tax credit landscapes have diverged significantly in response to the federal reforms3. While British Columbia expressly aligned its provincial SR&ED tax credit with the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit, ECPC inclusion, $15,000,000–$75,000,000 phase-out range, and restored capital expenditure rules—while making its provincial credit permanent in B.C. Budget 2026—other provinces have charted independent courses3. Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished its legacy suite of R&D salary, university, pre-competitive, and consortium tax credits, replacing them with the unified, refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% on excess expenditures, alongside capital property eligibility8. Saskatchewan expanded its refundable CCPC threshold from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 at a 10% rate (within a $1,000,000 total annual credit cap), whereas Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon retained their distinct statutory limits and structures3.
1. Legislative Architecture and the 2024–2026 Federal SR&ED Reforms
1.1 Statutory Foundation Under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program is codified within the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA" or the "Act") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations")4. The program is jointly overseen by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical and financial compliance, issues interpretive policies, and processes tax filings2.

The federal statutory architecture operates through a dual-incentive mechanism comprising an immediate income tax deduction and an investment tax credit20. First, under the Immediate Income Deduction and Indefinite Pool Carryforward (Section 37 of the ITA), subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to deduct allowable current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada (or qualifying foreign salary/wages within the 10% statutory cap under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)) in computing business income for the taxation year7. Any portion of the Section 37 expenditure pool not deducted in the current taxation year may be carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years, subject to loss restriction event rules under subsection 37(6.1)18. Second, under the Investment Tax Credits (Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA), subsections 127(5) and 127(9) permit taxpayers to earn an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year1. Under section 127.1, qualifying corporations and eligible entities may receive all or a portion of their unused ITCs as a direct cash refund, while non-refundable or unrefunded ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable1.

body.text: 1.2 Chronology and Enactment of the 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms

Following public consultations initiated by the Department of Finance in early 2024 regarding modernizing Canada's R&D investment climate, the federal government rolled out a multi-stage legislative expansion that received Royal Assent in March 20262. In the first stage, on December 16, 2024, the federal government tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), proposing four major structural changes effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (and for capital property acquired or lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024)9. First, the FES proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,0009. Second, it proposed increasing the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds for CCPCs (on an associated group basis) from the legacy $10,000,000–$50,000,000 range to $15,000,000–$75,000,0009. Third, it proposed expanding access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), subject to a straight-line phase-out based on average consolidated gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, while allowing CCPCs to elect to use this gross revenue phase-out structure instead of taxable capital9. Fourth, it proposed restoring the pre-2014 eligibility rules for SR&ED capital expenditures (both All or Substantially All [ASA] depreciable property and Shared-Use Equipment [SUE]) and lease costs incurred after December 15, 20249.

In the second stage, following the release of draft legislative proposals on August 15, 202539, Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne presented the 2025 Federal Budget on November 4, 20259. Budget 2025 confirmed all SR&ED measures from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and further increased the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from the previously announced $4,500,000 to $6,000,000, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 20249. Budget 2025 projected a net fiscal impact of $293,000,000 over five years (2025–2026 to 2029–2030) for this expansion ($3,000,000 in 2025–2026; $70,000,000 in 2026–2027; $85,000,000 in 2027–2028; $65,000,000 in 2028–2029; and $70,000,000 in 2029–2030)10.

In the third stage, on March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 received Royal Assent, formally codifying the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 phase-out thresholds, ECPC eligibility, and restored capital/lease expenditure eligibility into the Income Tax Act2. Shortly thereafter, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval program through My Business Account, allowing qualifying businesses with under $25,000,000 in gross business income to obtain upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks prior to starting work or filing a claim2.

body.text: 2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Technical Eligibility Framework
2.1 The Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The gateway to all federal and provincial SR&ED tax incentives is the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act16. Eligibility of work is determined strictly under subsection 248(1) before any expenditure rules under section 37 or section 127 are applied16. Under the preamble to the definition in subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis"24 and that falls into one of three core categories of work (paragraphs (a), (b), or (c)), plus eligible support work (paragraph (d)), while explicitly excluding seven enumerated categories of commercial or routine activity (paragraphs (e) through (k))24.

Under paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research), eligible work encompasses investigations undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view24. Basic research is typically conducted in laboratory settings or via third-party payments to universities, research institutes, and scientific consortia, with results often published in scientific journals (for example, theoretical and experimental investigations demonstrating the existence and measuring the mass and charge of elementary particles such as the electron)45. Under paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research), eligible work encompasses investigations undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view24. Like basic research, applied research seeks to advance scientific understanding, but is directed toward a practical objective (for example, investigating the properties of semiconductors and how electrons behave within them with the goal of eventually creating a semiconductor amplifier, prior to developing a specific device)45. Under paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development), eligible work encompasses investigations undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto24. Experimental development accounts for the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada46. It does not require advancing pure scientific knowledge; rather, it advances technology—the practical application of scientific knowledge and engineering principles—including incremental technological improvements to existing materials, devices, products, or processes24.

Furthermore, paragraph 248(1)(d) (Support Work) includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only eight exhaustive statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research24. Support work under paragraph (d) is never eligible as SR&ED on a standalone basis24. To qualify, it must satisfy two mandatory statutory conditions: it must be (i) commensurate with the needs, and (ii) directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer24.
2.2 Statutory Exclusions Under Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Even where a project involves genuine experimental development, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes work with respect to seven statutory categories from the definition of SR&ED16. The table below details each statutory exclusion and its operational boundary against eligible paragraph (d) support work.

All commercial market surveys, customer preference testing, and promotional demonstrations are excluded24.

Routine QA/QC testing for commercial production is excluded; however, non-routine testing conducted specifically to test an SR&ED hypothesis qualifies as paragraph (d) support work24.

Disqualifies behavioural, economic, financial, or market-analytics research (a frequent audit exclusion for data analytics companies)16.

body.text: As emphasized in the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (which replaced the archived Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy on August 13, 2021)24, the critical factor distinguishing eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as "data collection" or "testing") from excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") is purpose24. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically and directly to perform the scientific research or experimental development work, it qualifies as paragraph (d) support work24. Conversely, if testing or data collection is performed to support routine business operations, it is statutorily excluded24.
2.3 The Five-Question Judicial Test vs. The CRA's "Why" and "How" Administrative Framework

In Canadian tax law, the substantive evaluation of whether an activity satisfies subsection 248(1) is governed by the five-question legal test established by Chief Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), and formally adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2021 FCA 8826:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?26
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?26
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?26
Did the process result in a technological advancement?26
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?26

body.text: In its August 2021 Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives, the CRA synthesized the five Northwest Hydraulic questions into a two-part administrative methodology known as the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement24.

The "Why" Requirement corresponds to Northwest Hydraulic Questions 1 and 4 (Technological Uncertainty and Technological Advancement) and mandates that work be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement24. The focus must be on generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories or prediction models) rather than routine factual knowledge (such as standard measurements)24. A scientific or technological uncertainty arises when the existing scientific or technological knowledge base—combining the company's internal technical resources and publicly available sources accessible to competent professionals in the field—is insufficient to determine whether a specified objective can be achieved or how to achieve it11. Recognizing scientific or technological uncertainty marks the starting point of SR&ED work, and attempting to resolve this uncertainty satisfies the "Why" requirement24. Characteristics of problems indicating that available technological knowledge is insufficient include situations where existing design methods are not applicable, requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards, too many variables or unknowns interact, parameters or conditions fall outside the normal operating range, the nature of the problem is evolving, data is not readily available, or interlocking system constraints prevent predictable solutions ("system uncertainty")24. Crucially, acquiring available knowledge or know-how through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve technological advancement24. Conversely, success or failure in achieving the project's commercial or technical objectives is irrelevant: the rejection of a hypothesis through testing is itself a valid technological advancement because it advances understanding by ruling out an approach (Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, [1999] 4 C.T.C. 2701)24.

The "How" Requirement corresponds to Northwest Hydraulic Questions 2, 3, and 5 (Hypothesis Formulation, Systematic Investigation, and Contemporaneous Record-Keeping) and mandates that work be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis24. Under the CRA guidelines, a systematic investigation requires four sequential elements: generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the problem; testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change as a result of testing); developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses24. Trial-and-error tinkering or unguided adjustments without formulating and testing hypotheses fail the "How" requirement11.
2.4 Special Operational Scenarios: Prototypes, Pilot Plants, Custom Products, and Commercial Production Runs

Under the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy and SR&ED During Production Runs Policy47, claimants must carefully segregate eligible experimental development from commercial asset construction. When developing a prototype—an original trial model constructed to test a concept or hypothesis—expenditures relating to the labour and materials used in designing, constructing, and testing the prototype qualify as current SR&ED expenditures26. Because a prototype usually has no commercial application or limited residual value once tested, input materials are in most cases treated as materials consumed in SR&ED47. However, if input materials forming part of the prototype or subsequent copies of a prototype retain commercial value, they are treated as materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED and become subject to ITC recapture rules if later sold or converted to commercial use32.

Similarly, during the development and operation of a pilot plant, eligible expenditures include the labour used and materials consumed or transformed in resolving the technological uncertainties of developing equipment for incorporation into the pilot plant, as well as the labour and materials consumed or transformed in operating the pilot plant to resolve technological uncertainties47. In contrast, work and expenditures that would normally be associated with developing a commercial plant had the technology already existed do not qualify47. Where SR&ED is undertaken during the development of a custom product or commercial asset, the claimant must segregate the SR&ED work from the commercial work and allocate costs accordingly56. The CRA explicitly prohibits claiming the entire material cost of a commercial asset as "materials transformed" with the intention of simply applying ITC recapture later; only the cost of materials consumed or transformed directly in the prosecution of the SR&ED portion of the work is allowable56. Any production beyond what is strictly required for the SR&ED is classified as ineligible excess production57.
3. Federal SR&ED Tax Incentives: Rates, Thresholds, Phase-Outs, Refundability, and Carryovers
3.1 The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, reported in Part 3, Section C of Form T661, all allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada are accumulated in a tax mechanism known as the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures20. When a corporate claimant performs SR&ED related to a business actively engaged in by a related corporation (for instance, a subsidiary conducting R&D for its parent's active business), subsection 37(1.1) deems the SR&ED to relate to the claimant's business7. Conversely, subsection 37(4) and Regulation 2902(c) strictly prohibit any Section 37 deduction for expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED22.
Under subsection 37(1) (Increases to the Pool), the pool is increased each taxation year by six statutory items:

items: Allowable current SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada under paragraph 37(1)(a), including directly engaged salaries and wages, permissible foreign salaries up to the 10% cap, materials consumed or transformed, post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs, 100% of arm's length and non-arm's length SR&ED contracts, third-party payments, and Traditional Method overhead7;

Allowable SR&ED capital expenditures on depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, that meet the ASA (90%+) test under paragraph 37(1)(b)—note that Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) are never included in the Section 37 deductible pool2;
Repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) (Line 445)20;
Prior-year negative pool balances included in income under paragraph 12(1)(v) and added back to the pool under paragraph 37(1)(c.1)22;
Pool balances transferred upon an amalgamation (section 87) or corporate wind-up (section 88) (Line 452)1; and
The amount of any SR&ED ITC recaptured in the immediately preceding taxation year under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3) (Line 453)20.

body.text: Under paragraphs 37(1)(d) through (h) (Decreases to the Pool), the pool is reduced by: government assistance and non-government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received on or before the filing-due date under paragraph 37(1)(d) (Lines 429, 431, 432)7; provincial super-allowance benefit amounts under paragraph 37(1)(d.1)22; federal SR&ED ITCs applied against Part I tax or refunded in the preceding taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e) (Line 435)—except for partnerships, where allocated ITCs reduce the partnership's Section 37 pool in the same fiscal period under subsection 127(12.1)7; proceeds of disposition / recapture on the sale of SR&ED capital assets (Line 440)2; amounts deducted from the pool in previous taxation years under paragraph 37(1)(f)22; and insolvency deductions under section 61.3 (paragraph 37(1)(f.1))22. If these reductions exceed the pool additions and opening balance, resulting in a negative pool balance at year-end, the negative amount must be included in net income for tax purposes for that year under paragraph 12(1)(v), which simultaneously adds that amount back to the pool under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) so that the opening pool balance for the next taxation year is nil (zero)22.

For corporations and individuals, deducting an amount from a positive Section 37 pool balance (Line 460) is completely optional, and any undeducted balance (Line 470) carries forward indefinitely to future taxation years (the subsequent deduction of an already-pooled amount is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, provided the expenditures were originally reported on time on Form T661)20. However, a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance: under paragraph 96(1)(e.1), the partnership's entire pool balance at the end of its fiscal period must be fully deducted in computing the partnership's net income for that year22. Furthermore, under paragraph 96(1)(g), a limited partner's share of a partnership business loss created or increased by deducting the Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool is disallowed to the limited partner (and does not become a limited partnership loss or non-capital loss)25. Finally, when a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (a loss restriction event), its Section 37 pool is reduced to nil under paragraph 37(1)(h) and streamed under subsection 37(6.1): the pre-acquisition pool can only be deducted in future years if the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of income from that same business or a similar business22.

body.text: Added to subsection 127(9) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a corporation qualifies as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) if, throughout the taxation year, it satisfies three cumulative conditions: (1) it is resident in Canada; (2) a class of its shares is listed on a designated stock exchange (or it has elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) it is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons1. Additionally, Canadian-resident subsidiary corporations of which all or substantially all (90% or more) of the shares are owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC regime, sharing the corporate group's expenditure limit9.
3.3 The $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the maximum annual Expenditure Limit is $6,000,000 (doubled from the pre-December 16, 2024 limit of $3,000,000)1. This $6,000,000 limit must be shared among all associated corporations in a taxation year by filing an allocation agreement on Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) pursuant to subsection 127(10.3)16. Two distinct phase-out mechanisms govern the reduction of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit for scaling companies1.

Under Method A (Prior-Year Taxable Capital Phase-Out — Default for CCPCs), for CCPCs that do not elect into the gross revenue method, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation (together with all associated corporations) reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated (becomes nil) when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 (expanded from the pre-December 16, 2024 phase-out range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000)1. Expressed mathematically, the post-December 15, 2024 linear phase-out across the $60,000,000 range between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 is $6,000,000 × (($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000), where A is nil if prior-year associated taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,0001. Thus, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1 (for example, at $45,000,000 of taxable capital, the expenditure limit is $3,000,000; at $75,000,000, it is $0)1. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the legacy formula phased out the $3,000,000 limit where A was nil at or below $10,000,000 and equalled the lesser of $40,000,000 and the excess over $10,000,000, eliminating the limit at $50,000,000.)9

Under Method B (Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out — Mandatory for ECPCs, Elective for CCPCs), the post-December 15, 2024 legislation introduced a gross revenue phase-out structure for ECPCs and granted CCPCs the statutory option to elect on a prescribed form to have their $6,000,000 expenditure limit determined under this gross revenue formula instead of the taxable capital formula1. Under this method, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when the corporation's average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,000 or greater1. For corporate groups preparing consolidated financial statements, gross revenue is the amount reported in the group's annual financial statements presented to shareholders at the highest level of consolidation, and all members of the corporate group must share access to the expenditure limit9. For standalone corporations not in a group, gross revenue is the amount reported in annual financial statements prepared in accordance with GAAP presented to shareholders9. This election allows capital-intensive CCPCs whose taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 (for example, due to equity or debt financings) but whose three-year average gross revenue is below $15,000,000 to preserve their full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit9.
3.4 Carryback, Carryforward, and Acquisition of Control Rules for ITCs

Where an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit is non-refundable (or where a claimant does not claim a refund), subsection 127(5) and the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) govern carryover periods1. Unused ITCs earned in the current taxation year may be carried back 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the lesser of the unused current-year ITC and the amount by which Part I tax otherwise payable in that prior year exceeds that prior year's ITC) and carried forward 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I federal tax otherwise payable1. Under subsection 127(5), if minimum tax under Division E.1 applies to an individual, the ITC deduction cannot exceed the amount by which Part I tax otherwise payable exceeds the taxpayer's minimum amount determined under section 127.514.

Any ITC applied against Part I tax or refunded in a taxation year is deemed deducted against Part I tax under subsection 127.1(3), reducing the ITC balance available for carryforward or carryback and reducing the taxpayer's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the subsequent taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e)1. For partnerships, because a partnership is not a person/taxpayer, ITCs are computed at the partnership level and allocated at the end of the partnership's fiscal period to eligible active/general partners under subsection 127(8) (specified members—including limited partners and passive partners not regularly, continuously, and substantially engaged in the partnership's business—are strictly prohibited from receiving any partnership SR&ED ITCs under paragraph 127(8)(b)), and the allocated ITC reduces the partnership's Section 37 pool in the same year under subsection 127(12.1)4. Furthermore, in All Colour Chemicals, the Tax Court confirmed that because subsection 127(8) overrides subsection 127(10.1), CCPC partners of a partnership earn ITCs at the 15% basic rate rather than the 35% enhanced CCPC rate55. Finally, upon an acquisition of control (loss restriction event), subsections 127(9.1) and 127(9.2) restrict the carryforward of pre-acquisition ITCs and the carryback of post-acquisition ITCs, whereas on an amalgamation (section 87, paragraphs 87(2)(j.6), (l), and (qq)) or wind-up of a subsidiary into a parent (section 88, paragraphs 88(1)(e.2) and (e.3)), the continuing or parent corporation is deemed to be a continuation of the predecessor or subsidiary for calculating ITCs at the end of taxation years ending after the wind-up (though the parent cannot carry back the subsidiary's ITCs to parent taxation years prior to the wind-up)1.

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, a claimant must select each taxation year whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162)20. If a claimant fails to select a method on Form T661, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method59.

(Note: While older text on Line 820 of certain archived T4088 guides references 65% with 2013 calendar-day adjustments20, Table 1 of T4088 and the CRA's revised Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy explicitly confirm that the statutory rate under Regulation 2900(4) is 55% of the salary base16.)

Under Regulations 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) (calculated in Part 5 of Form T661, Lines 810 to 820), the salary base is narrower than total SR&ED payroll16. For non-specified employees (Lines 810–814), the salary base equals their directly engaged SR&ED salaries and wages minus all taxable benefits, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current taxation year (Line 310)16. For specified employees (Lines 850–860 and 816), the amount that a claimant can include in the salary base for each specified employee is restricted by Regulation 2900(7) to the lesser of: (1) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year); (2) the actual SR&ED salary or wages spent by the specified employee (Line 852 × Line 854 % of time spent on SR&ED); or (3) 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual using the formula 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), where A is the YMPE and B is the number of days employed in the taxation year (Line 858, with no proration for days during the year the employee was not a specified employee)16. If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (or deemed associated individuals/partnerships under Regulation 2900(10)) in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the total salary base inclusion across the associated group cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE under Regulation 2900(8)16.
4.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, YMPE Caps, and the 10% Foreign Work Rule

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy and subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "salary or wages" means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act23. It includes regular salaries, wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, honorariums, director's/management fees, commissions, and cash outlays (or reasonable actual cost estimates excluding GST/HST/PST) for taxable benefits (such as automobile benefits, housing/board, or group term life insurance), as well as bonuses and profit-based remuneration for non-specified employees23. In Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc., 2016 TCC 183, the Tax Court confirmed that performance remuneration tied to sales volume paid to an employee fell within the subsection 248(1) definition of salary or wages26. Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages never include the employer's share of related payroll benefits (which can only be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method), extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits (disallowed by legislation after November 14, 2005, following Alcatel, 2005 TCC 149), or retiring allowances23.

Only the portion of an employee's salary or wages corresponding to actual time spent directly engaged in SR&ED (under the Proxy Method) or directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED (under the Traditional Method) is allowable20. Whether an employee is directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED is a question of fact based on actual tasks performed rather than job titles; however, employees who spend all or substantially all (at least 90%) of their time directly engaged in SR&ED are deemed to spend 100% of their time on SR&ED20. For specified employees—defined in subsection 248(1) as employees who do not deal at arm's length with the claimant or who are specified shareholders owning (together with non-arm's length persons) 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation23—two strict statutory restrictions apply to their direct salary claims on Line 305 and Line 309: (1) bonuses and remuneration based on profits are completely excluded23; and (2) under subsections 37(9.2) and 37(9.3), their maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages expenditure is capped at 5 times the YMPE prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the taxation year (5 × YMPE × (B ÷ 365))7. Where a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations, no amount may be claimed unless the associated corporations file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) accompanied by a certified copy of the board of directors' resolution on or before their respective SR&ED reporting deadlines7.

body.text: Two additional timing and territorial rules govern SR&ED salaries and wages. First, under the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4)), any SR&ED salary or wages incurred in a taxation year but not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year20. They must be identified on Line 315 of Form T661 in the year incurred and can only be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid20. Second, under the 10% Limit on SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)), enacted after LGL Ltd. v. The Queen (which held that work physically outside Canada—other than inside Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone under s. 37(1.3)—was ineligible), permissible salary or wages paid to Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED outside Canada (reported on Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees) are deemed made in Canada if: (a) the foreign work is directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant; (b) the salary or wages are not subject to income or profits tax from another country; and (c) the deductible foreign salary/wages do not exceed 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages paid to employees for SR&ED directly undertaken in Canada (Lines 300 + 305) in that taxation year7.
4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Regulation 2900(2)(a))

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA, and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations, a claimant may claim the cost of materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada20. To qualify as "materials for SR&ED," the raw materials, substances, or items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a thing (an intermediate product, by-product, or final product) on which SR&ED is performed or that results from the SR&ED58. Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, and their claimable cost is the laid-down cost (invoice cost plus customs and excise duties, transportation, storage, and acquisition costs; or for internally manufactured inventory, laid-down cost plus direct labour and applicable production overhead, even under the Proxy Method; for non-arm's length purchases, subsection 127(11.6) limits the ITC-eligible cost to the cost incurred by the non-arm's length supplier excluding profit)58. Crucially, the cost of materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed in prosecuting SR&ED (not when purchased into inventory) and must be paid within 180 days of year-end under subsection 127(26)58.

Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials that are destroyed, rendered virtually valueless, or disposed of as waste with no residual or resale value as a result of prosecuting SR&ED (for example, galvanized metal parts destroyed during testing, ink and cardboard boxes rendered worthless in printing tests, seed, agar, fungal growth media, fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides applied to experimental test plots, or process water that enters the body of an experimental product)58. Materials consumed are not subject to ITC recapture unless subsequent proceeds (such as insurance proceeds) exceed 10% of the cost of the materials32. Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials or components incorporated or transformed into a prototype, experimental production run, custom product, or commercial asset that retains value after the SR&ED47. Subsequent sale or conversion to commercial use of that object within 20 years triggers ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36), unless proceeds from selling the experimental product are less than 10% of its total cost, which the CRA treats as scrap sales exempt from recapture32. Conversely, general utilities (electricity, natural gas, heating oil, utility or boiler feed water), cleaning supplies, used lubricants, CDs/DVDs, and broken or used laboratory glassware (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes) do not compose the body of a thing and cannot be claimed as materials on Line 320/325 (they may only be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental)58.
4.4 Subcontractors (Arm's Length vs. Non-Arm's Length) and Third-Party Payments
Canadian SR&ED law establishes distinct statutory rules for arm's length SR&ED contracts, non-arm's length SR&ED contracts, and third-party payments28.

Under Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340 — Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), when a claimant contracts an arm's length party to perform SR&ED in Canada on behalf of the claimant, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is deductible in the Section 37 pool, but only 80% of the contract expenditure qualifies for the federal ITC pursuant to subsection 127(9) (a 20% reduction is deducted on Line 529 of Form T661)16. Under the Taxable Supplier Rule (reported on Line 528), a current SR&ED contract expenditure paid or payable to a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier (i.e., a foreign contractor without a Canadian permanent establishment) is excluded from qualified expenditures and earns 0% ITC20. Claimants must report the names and CRA Business Numbers (BN) of all contractors on Lines 268 and 269 of Form T66120.

Under Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Line 345), where a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length performer (under section 251), the payer's contract expenditure is an allowable Section 37 deduction (Line 345), but is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) (deducted on Line 541)20. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures (and the payment from the NAL payer is excluded from the definition of "contract payment" so it does not reduce the performer's pool), OR the NAL performer and payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) to transfer all or a portion of the performer's qualified expenditures (including its PPA, capped at the contract amount) to the payer (reported on Line 508 / Line 544)20. Note that because a partnership is not a "taxpayer," a partnership cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures on Form T1146 under subsection 127(13)25.

Under Third-Party Payments (Line 370 & Form T1263 — Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii)), a claimant may claim payments (including direct funding or payments in kind valued at fair market value) made to six statutory categories of third-party entities ("A to F entities") for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the claimant, provided the claimant is entitled to exploit the results7. The six entity types are: A entity (a corporation resident in Canada, s. 37(1)(a)(i.1)—claimable only in the year the SR&ED is performed); B entity (an approved association, s. 37(1)(a)(ii)); C entity (an approved university, college, research institute, or similar institution, s. 37(1)(a)(ii)); D entity (a non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j), s. 37(1)(a)(ii)); E entity (an approved granting council making payments to B, C, or D entities, s. 37(1)(a)(ii)); and F entity (a paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporation carrying on basic or applied pre-competitive research in Canada, s. 37(1)(a)(iii))68. Like arm's length contracts, 100% of a third-party payment is deductible in the Section 37 pool and 80% qualifies for the federal ITC (reduced by 20% on Line 529)20. Claimants must complete and attach Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development) for every third-party payment claimed27.

The CRA's policies distinguish an SR&ED contract (Line 340) from a third-party payment (Line 370) across five criteria: in a contract, (1) the SR&ED work is controlled by the payer, (2) rights to the work are exclusive to the payer, (3) the contract is usually limited to one payer, (4) the work has a specific commercial focus, and (5) tax treatment is accrual; whereas in a third-party payment, the institution controls the research, the payer merely obtains a right to exploit results, multiple funders often participate, and payments to B–E entities are recognized in the year paid59.
4.5 Overhead, Cloud Computing, Bandwidth, and Software Licences

Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA and Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)), overhead and other indirect costs can only be claimed on Line 360 if the taxpayer elects the Traditional Method20. Under Regulation 2900(2)(c), an expenditure (or portion thereof) must satisfy two cumulative tests to qualify on Line 360: (1) the Directly Related Test (a direct connection without an intervening step to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED); and (2) the Incremental Test (the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred)36.

Eligible Line 360 overhead items (when directly related and incremental) include: the employer's share of related payroll benefits for hands-on/direct SR&ED employees; clerical and administrative support salaries (e.g., HR, accounting, purchasing staff providing direct services aiding ongoing SR&ED—though related benefits, travel, or training for clerical/support staff are disallowed because their link is indirect); incremental utilities consumed directly in SR&ED (e.g., variable electricity used to run SR&ED equipment); identifiable long-distance telephone charges for SR&ED; travel and lodging in Canada for customer-site testing; SR&ED staff training in Canada; technical periodical subscriptions; clinical trial volunteer fees; moving expenses to relocate SR&ED employees within Canada (unlike headhunter fees, recruiting ads, or immigration/visa costs, which are ineligible); and retiring allowances proportional to an employee's exclusive SR&ED service36. Conversely, fixed monthly telephone, cellular, or internet fees, fixed-cost maintenance contracts, post-project waste disposal costs, and prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902 (legal/accounting fees, interest, entertainment, advertising, convention attendance, professional membership dues, fines, and fees paid to consultants or accountants for preparing SR&ED claims) are strictly disallowed28.

For cloud computing (e.g., AWS, Azure), dedicated bandwidth, and software licences, treatment depends on the calculation method and legal characterization19. Under the Traditional Method, metered, variable cloud computing costs incurred specifically to run SR&ED experiments or train experimental models qualify on Line 360 if directly related and incremental, whereas fixed baseline hosting fees fail the incremental test36. Under the Proxy Method, Line 360 overhead cannot be claimed separately; however, under the CRA's updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) and the Tax Court precedent in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 98 DTC 1877, costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for dedicated bandwidth or leased computing equipment (which relies on sophisticated optoelectronic/server equipment rather than General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture [GPOEF]) or software licences legally characterized as equipment leases qualify as lease expenditures if used ASA (≥90% operating time, 100% claimable) or primarily (>50% to <90% operating time, 50% claimable under the Proxy Method)19.
4.6 Restored Eligibility of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Enacted via Bill C-15 (following the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025), the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and equipment lease costs has been restored for depreciable property acquired (and available for use under subsection 37(1.2)) and lease payments first becoming payable after December 15, 20242. (Capital property acquired or lease costs incurred between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, remain ineligible; additionally, the former subsection 37(14)/(15) capital look-through rules no longer reduce post-December 15, 2024 contract or third-party payments.)2

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), All or Substantially All (ASA — 90% or More) Depreciable Capital Property (Line 390, Paragraph 37(1)(b)) covers new or used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, where, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either: (i) to use the property during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; or (ii) that all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada2. The capital cost (including purchase price, installation, customs/excise duties, and transportation, reported in Part 2 Lines 262–263 and Part 6 Box 782) is 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool (Line 390, deemed capital cost allowance under Regulation 1102(1)(d)) and must not be claimed on Schedule T2SCH82. Crucially, while both new and used depreciable property meeting the ASA test qualify for the 100% immediate income deduction in the Section 37 pool (Line 390), used depreciable property does NOT qualify for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits under Regulation 2902(b) (and must be subtracted on Line 535 in Part 4), unless refurbished by the vendor prior to sale to such a significant extent that it is considered "new" upon acquisition (or if refurbished by the claimant after acquisition, only the cost of the significant refurbishment qualifies)2. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning the 35% enhanced ITC, credits on new ASA capital property are refundable at 40% (yielding a 14% immediate cash refund: 40% × 35%), while land, leasehold interests in land, buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, inventory, and goodwill are permanently excluded2.

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Line 504 & Part 6C Box 792, Subsection 127(9)) applies to depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities2. To qualify as SUE (under both the Traditional and Proxy methods), the equipment must be new (never used or rented prior to acquisition), must not be General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (property intended at acquisition to be used during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing/processing facility and intended to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its expected useful life)2. SUE is not deductible in the Section 37 pool; instead, it is depreciated under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and earns ITCs on Line 504 based on actual operating time over two periods2:

items: First Term SUE: If the new equipment is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the "first period" (beginning when the equipment becomes available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition), 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowing costs under s. 21 and adjusted for non-arm's length costs under s. 127(11.6)) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC on Line 5042.

Second Term SUE: If the equipment qualified as First Term SUE and is used primarily (>50% of actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the "second period" (beginning at acquisition and ending at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition), an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC on Line 504 (up to 50% cumulative inclusion across both periods)2.

The Queen, 99 DTC 5669)9. Building rent is excluded under both methods (except for prescribed special-purpose buildings approved by the Department of Finance under Regulation 2903)19. Under the Proxy Method, lease costs for GPOEF and land are excluded; for all other SR&ED equipment, if used ASA (≥90% operating time) for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); if used primarily (>50% to <90% operating time), 50% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); if used ≤50%, 0% is claimable19. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used ASA (≥90% operating time), 100% is claimed as a lease cost (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)); if used less than 90% of the time, the actual SR&ED operating percentage (including for GPOEF or leased land) is claimable on Line 360 as overhead if directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II))2.
5. Assistance Reductions, Contract Payments, Non-Arm's Length Rules, and ITC Recapture
5.1 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments (Subsections 127(18)–(20) and Paragraph 37(1)(d))

Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (updated March 27, 2026), paragraph 37(1)(d), and subsections 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Lines 429, 431, 432) and the Part 4 qualified SR&ED expenditure pool (Lines 513 to 517) must be reduced dollar-for-dollar by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year4. Reductions are applied on a project-by-project basis down to nil (and any excess assistance over project expenditures in the Section 37 pool is included in income)29.

Government assistance (subsection 127(9)) encompasses any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax (including all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits), investment allowance, or other form of assistance from a government, municipality, Crown corporation, foreign government, or other public authority (an entity with a public duty, significant government control, and public-benefit use of profits), other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself15. In CAE Inc. v. His Majesty The King, 2022 FCA 178, and Her Majesty the Queen v. CCLC Technologies Inc., 96 DTC 6527 (FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal established that government loans or conditionally repayable contributions with below-market interest rates or conditional repayment terms that a commercial lender would not accept constitute government assistance in full, reducing SR&ED qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar26. Non-government assistance (subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x)) includes any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance from a private entity toward SR&ED costs4. Contract payments (subsection 127(9)) include amounts paid or payable to a claimant by an arm's length taxable supplier (or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or section 149 tax-exempt entity, excluding prescribed foreign government amounts routed through the Canadian Commercial Corporation) for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf29. However, as held in Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 773 (TCC), a fixed-price commercial contract for the sale of a product where the contractor bears the financial risk is ordinary revenue rather than an SR&ED contract payment21.

Where assistance or a contract payment exceeds the recipient's own qualified expenditures on a project, subsections 127(19) and 127(20) require the excess to reduce the qualified expenditures of non-arm's length group members performing the SR&ED, allocated using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length)4. Conversely, if a claimant formally renounces a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit on or before its income tax return filing-due date (6 months after year-end), the renounced credit does not reduce the federal Section 37 pool or Part 4 qualified expenditures15. Finally, when a claimant repays government or non-government assistance (or contract payments) that previously reduced its SR&ED pools, the repayment increases the Section 37 deductible pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) (Line 445) and is added on Line 560 of Form T661 to earn federal SR&ED ITCs in the year of repayment20.
5.2 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA, previously earned SR&ED ITCs are reversed (added directly to Part I federal tax payable) when four cumulative conditions are met: (1) the claimant acquired a particular property in the current taxation year or any of the 20 preceding taxation years (the 20-year lookback window under subsection 127(36)); (2) the cost of the property was claimed as a qualified SR&ED expenditure; (3) the cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC; and (4) the claimant disposes of (sells) or converts to commercial use the property (or another property incorporating it) during the taxation year1.

Recapture applies to materials transformed (Line 325, including experimental products, custom products, or animals/plants sold), restored ASA capital property (Line 390, acquired after December 15, 2024, as well as pre-2014 capital assets within the 20-year lookback), restored Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Line 504, when sold or converted ASA to commercial use), and tangible property (other than IP) acquired through an arm's length SR&ED contract (plus transferred expenditures under subsections 127(13) and 127(29))9. Conversely, no recapture ever applies to SR&ED salaries and wages, overhead, intellectual property (IP) sold or licensed commercially, non-arm's length transfers of ASA capital property that continue to be used ASA in SR&ED by the transferee (subsection 127(33)), materials consumed (unless insurance/recovery proceeds exceed 10% of cost), or scrap sales where proceeds or fair market value are less than 10% of the total cost of the experimental product31.

The amount of ITC recaptured and added to Part I tax payable is the lesser of: (i) the original federal ITC earned in respect of the property; and (ii) the applicable ITC rate multiplied by the Proceeds of Disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the property (if converted to commercial use or disposed of to a non-arm's length party)32. Any federal ITC recaptured in a taxation year is subsequently added back to the claimant's Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2) (Line 453 of Form T661)20.
