body.text: Since legislative amendments enacted in November 2005, there is no statutory mechanism or Ministerial discretion to extend the SR&ED reporting deadline11. If a claimant fails to file Form T661 containing the prescribed information (including the mandatory project narratives in Part 2 Lines 242–246 and any unpaid amounts on Line 315/520) on or before the reporting deadline, the expenditures are permanently disqualified as SR&ED expenditures: the claimant cannot deduct them under Section 37 and cannot earn any ITCs (Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2018 FCA 57; 1373744 Ontario Inc. o/a One Source Metal v. The Queen, 2009 TCC 511)26. If Form T661 is filed on time, but Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) is filed after the reporting deadline, the claimant may still include the allowable expenditures in the Section 37 deductible pool, but permanently loses all entitlement to earn any ITC on those expenditures (Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2016 FCA 301)26. Conversely, if Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 are filed on time without a T2 return, the statutory SR&ED deadline is satisfied, though processing is delayed until the T2 return is filed27. To mitigate deadline risk, the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy recommends filing SR&ED claims at least 90 days before the 18-month reporting deadline (within 15 months of year-end) so the CRA can conduct an initial completeness review and alert the claimant to any omissions before the deadline expires27. (Note that for non-arm's length agreements on Form T1145 and Form T1146, the agreement must be filed on or before the transferor's income tax return filing-due date, or within the period in which the transferor or transferee may serve a Notice of Objection for that year.)27
6.3 The Optional CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Launched on April 1, 2026, following the enactment of Bill C-15, the CRA's Pre-Claim Approval process is an optional program enabling businesses to have their planned (or recently started) R&D projects evaluated by the CRA to confirm whether the work satisfies SR&ED technical eligibility requirements before incurring significant R&D costs or submitting an annual tax claim2.

To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, both the business and the project must satisfy specific criteria42. At the business level, the applicant must: (1) be a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), another Canadian corporation, or a partnership; (2) have gross business income of less than $25,000,000; and (3) be in good standing with the CRA42. At the project level, the planned project must: (4) not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim; and (5) not involve issues currently under litigation42.

The application process follows three sequential steps: first, the claimant confirms eligibility and requests a case number (and may book a one-on-one information session with a CRA representative via OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca); second, the claimant answers technical questions about the project and compiles supporting project planning documents; and third, the claimant uploads the application through My Business Account2. The CRA provides a formal determination within eight weeks2. When the claimant later files its annual Form T661 including projects that received Pre-Claim Approval (provided the work executed did not differ significantly from the approved plan), the CRA may select the claim for an expenditure-only review and generally processes the claim within 90 calendar days of receiving the complete claim69.
7. CRA Audit Procedures, Penalties, and Dispute Resolution
7.1 CRA Service Standards and Coordinated Review Workflow (RTA and FR)

When an SR&ED claim is received by the CRA, it is routed through automated risk assessment and screening69. For complete refundable SR&ED claims that are accepted as filed without a review, the CRA's published service standard has historically been 60 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (with industry advisory guides noting a 45-day CRA administrative target beginning in April 2026 for timely-filed claims not selected for review)69. For refundable SR&ED claims selected for review, the CRA's official service standard is 180 calendar days from the date the CRA receives the complete claim, which the CRA commits to meeting 90% of the time (reduced to 90 calendar days for expenditure-only reviews of claims granted Pre-Claim Approval)69. There is no service standard timeframe for non-refundable SR&ED claims selected for review69.

As codified in the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, Financial Claim Review Manual – Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers, and The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), a coordinated SR&ED review is executed jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (evaluating technical eligibility under subsection 248(1)) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (verifying allowable and qualified expenditures under sections 37 and 127) across three structured steps69:

items: Step 1 — Start of the Review and Initial Contact: The RTA or FR contacts the claimant by telephone and sends an Initial Claimant Contact Letter providing reviewer contact information, confirming the claimant's official language of choice (English or French), identifying the specific projects and financial issues selected for review, confirming available supporting documentation and electronic transfer methods (such as My Business Account or Electronic Transfer of Accounting Data [ETAD]), and scheduling the review meeting69. Under Compliance Programs Branch Communiqués AD-10-01 to AD-10-03, if requested documentation is not provided by the initial deadline, the RTA may grant a 15-day extension upon request, plus an additional 15 days if responses are incomplete; any extension beyond 30 total days requires reasonable grounds and approval from the Research and Technology Manager (RTM)71.

Step 2 — The Review Meeting, Technical Interviews, Tour of Premises, and Evidence Review: The RTA and FR conduct technical and financial interviews with key R&D performers and accounting personnel, tour the facilities (either virtually via screen-sharing/video or on-site), and examine contemporaneous supporting evidence ticked on Lines 270 to 282 of Form T661 (dated test logs, source code commit histories, engineering drawings, photographs, videos, scrap, or physical prototypes)69. Under the Claim Review Manual, the RTA must consult the RTM before recommending disallowance due to lack of information, before issuing an unfavourable decision without an on-site visit (unless the claim is in a field like IT with no physical artifacts and an alternative meeting is agreed upon, is in a remote location, or is clearly excluded under paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k)), or where penalties, suspected fraud, or "better books and records" letters are contemplated71. RTAs are strictly forbidden from negotiating eligibility percentages or encouraging claimants to withdraw projects as part of a bargaining trade-off71.

Step 3 — Review Findings, Proposal Package (30-Day Window), and Final Assessment: At the conclusion of the review, the RTA prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report (recorded in Section D.2 of the Financial Review Report [FRR]) and the FR computes the expenditure adjustments69. If adjustments (or penalties) are proposed, the CRA sends a Proposal Package comprising the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a Proposal Letter, and a Summary of Adjustments69. The claimant has 30 calendar days to submit written representations and additional evidence (or may sign a written waiver of the 30-day waiting period)69. After reviewing any representations, the FR completes the signed standard FRR (a Short FRR is prohibited whenever the claimant disagrees, submits written representations, plans to file a Notice of Objection, or settles a complex issue) along with assessing forms T7W-9 / T7W-C and Form T99A (and prepares a Headquarters package if permanent income changes exceed ±$2,000,000 or permanent tax/TEBA-NPV changes exceed ±$400,000), and the CRA issues a final letter and Notice of Assessment or Reassessment69.

body.text: 7.2 Civil and Criminal Penalties Governing SR&ED Claims
Three distinct statutory penalty provisions govern non-compliant or fraudulent SR&ED filings under the Income Tax Act:

First, under Subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) (Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty — $1,000), if a claimant uses one or more external claim preparers to prepare any technical or financial aspect of Form T661 (excluding mere software data entry), Part 9 of Form T661 (Lines 935–975) requires full disclosure of each preparer's name (Line 940), Business Number (Line 945), billing arrangement code (Line 950: percentage/contingency fee, hourly/daily rate, or flat fee), billing rate (Line 955), other billing arrangements (Line 960), and total fee paid, payable, or expected to be paid (Line 965)33. (Where a preparer wishes to keep its fee confidential from the claimant's staff, the CRA allows an optional two-step filing procedure where Lines 950–965 are left blank on the main return submission and filed simultaneously on a separate paper copy of Parts 1 and 9 sent directly to the Tax Centre.)34 While missing or inaccurate Part 9 information does not invalidate the SR&ED claim itself, subsection 162(5.1) imposes a $1,000 penalty if any required Part 9 information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate27. Under subsection 162(5.2), the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable for the $1,000 penalty, unless the preparer establishes a due diligence defence under subsection 162(5.3) showing it exercised the degree of care, diligence, and skill of a reasonably prudent person in comparable circumstances33.

Second, under Subsections 163(2) and 163(3) (Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims — 50%) and the CRA's revised Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), if a person knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes, participates in, assents to, or acquiesces in a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim, the penalty is the greater of $100 and 50% of the sum of35:

items: Paragraph 163(2)(a): The understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (arising either from deducting non-business/personal/false expenses in the Section 37 pool or from deducting an overstated ITC against Part I tax in the current, carryback, or carryforward years, with overstated amounts deemed deducted first, and computed under subsection 163(2.1) even if the corporation is in a net loss position); PLUS35

Paragraph 163(2)(d): The entire refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the taxpayer35. (From CRA Policy Examples 2 & 3: If a CCPC knowingly overstates SR&ED salaries by $200,000 under the Proxy Method, that generates an overstated PPA of $110,000 [55% × $200,000], totalling $310,000 in overstated qualified expenditures and $108,500 in overstated 35% ITC [35% × $310,000], resulting in a 50% gross negligence penalty of $54,250 [50% × $108,500]; whereas a separate $20,000 material disallowance caused by an honest oversight on the same return is excluded from the penalty calculation if Part I tax is reduced, though under paragraph 163(2)(d) when a gross negligence penalty applies to a refundable ITC refund claim, the CRA policy notes the penalty is calculated on the overstated refundable ITC refund claimed.)35 Crucially, under subsection 163(3), the statutory burden of proof rests on the Minister (CRA) to prove on a balance of probabilities that the false statement resulted from knowledge or gross negligence (conspicuous carelessness or wilful blindness) rather than an ordinary mistake35.

body.text: Third, under Section 163.2 (Third-Party Civil Penalties) and Subsection 239(1.1) (Criminal Offences for Tax Fraud), tax preparers who fabricate claims face civil penalties under section 163.274, while taxpayers and directors who submit falsified invoices or deceptive statements to claim SR&ED refunds commit a criminal offence under paragraphs 239(1.1)(a) and (c) punishable under paragraph 239(1.1)(g) by a mandatory fine of 50% to 200% of the excess credit or refund claimed (plus potential imprisonment)26. In Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc. / Maged Elhami and Shady Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684 (aff'd SCC 2018), where the defendants fabricated $4,500,000 in backdated subcontractor invoices from an innocent third party (Pyro Genesis) to claim $1,324,294 in SR&ED ITCs, the Court of Québec fined each of the three co-defendants $1,324,294 ($662,147 per count across two counts—totalling nearly $4,000,000 across the three defendants) even though the CRA caught the scheme during audit and paid out $026.
7.3 Administrative Dispute Resolution, Formal Objections, and Tax Court Appeals
Under the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns and The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, claimants have a structured four-step recourse mechanism when disputes arise49:

items: Step 1 — Resolve with the RTA and FR: Engage directly with the assigned Research and Technology Advisor and Financial Reviewer during the review or within the 30-day Proposal Package response window to clarify technical facts and submit additional documentation69.
Step 2 — Escalate to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and Financial Review Manager (FRM): If disagreements persist with the reviewers, request a meeting with their immediate managers69.

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review: Following receipt of the Proposal Package, if concerns have still not been adequately addressed by the reviewers and their managers, request a formal Administrative Review by senior SR&ED management to verify that SR&ED legislation, policies, procedures, and due process were properly followed (this is a due-process and policy compliance review rather than a second technical audit by new reviewers)69.

Step 4 — File a Formal Notice of Objection (90 Days) and Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada: Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the corporation has 90 calendar days from the date the Notice was sent (mailed or electronically posted) to serve a formal Notice of Objection to the Minister (CRA Appeals Division) under paragraph 165(1)(b) of the ITA26. Under subsections 166.1(7) and 166.2(5), an extension of time to object can only be requested within 1 year after the expiration of the initial 90-day period (1 year and 90 days total from the date the Notice of Assessment was sent); as confirmed in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146, once the CRA establishes mailing via automated Print-to-Mail affidavits under subsections 244(10) and 244(14), receipt is conclusively deemed on the mailing date under paragraph 248(7)(a), and the Tax Court has no legal jurisdiction to grant an extension past 1 year and 90 days26. Following the Appeals Division's decision (or after 90 days if Appeals has not responded), the taxpayer may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada26.

body.text: 8. Leading Canadian Jurisprudence and Tax Court of Canada Precedents

Because subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act sets out broad statutory principles, Canadian courts have developed an extensive body of binding jurisprudence governing SR&ED technical eligibility, evidentiary standards, filing deadlines, government assistance, and capital expenditure rules26. The table below synthesizes 34 leading Canadian SR&ED court decisions from 1988 through 202626.

headers: Judicial Holding & Practical Takeaway for SR&ED Audits

cells: Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363
Meaning of "systematic investigation"
Established that "systematic investigation" requires a structured, methodical plan where variables are controlled and tested; random trial-and-error without recorded parameters fails eligibility26.
Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen, 94 DTC 1725 (Docket 92-264)
Prototype vs. commercial asset & ASA timeframe

Held that a prototype green-sand refiner built to test technological feasibility qualified for SR&ED capital treatment ($10,851 in 1985, $104,084 in 1986, $90,148 in 1987) even though it succeeded, was patented, and was later used in commercial production; the 90% ASA test is assessed based on intent during the SR&ED phase, not with hindsight over full commercial life26.
CCLC Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 96 DTC 6527 (Docket A-801-95)
Government assistance vs. commercial investment

Held that funding from the Government of Alberta under an experimental Coal Research Agreement where the province could earn no net commercial profit constituted "government assistance" under s. 12(1)(x)(iv) and s. 127(9), reducing SR&ED qualified expenditures26.
Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 DTC 724
Purposive interpretation & commercial materials

Chief Justice Bowman articulated that Section 37 should be given a fair, large, and liberal interpretation to encourage R&D in Canada, and allowed textile materials used in experimental runs that were later sold (prompting Parliament to enact the s. 127(27) ITC recapture rules)21.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839
The Landmark 5-Question Test & System Uncertainty

Chief Justice Bowman established the canonical five-question test for SR&ED eligibility, defined "system uncertainty" (unpredictable interactions when integrating known components, allowing 4 of 5 hydraulic modelling projects), and confirmed that technological advancement includes incremental improvements26.
Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1877
Leased telecom bandwidth as lease of equipment
Held that payments for a dedicated telecommunications line used for SR&ED constituted an allowable lease of sophisticated optoelectronic equipment rather than general office overhead19.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, 99 DTC 5087 (Docket A-710-96)
Evidentiary standard & "repeatability"

Reversed the TCC and held that while documentary evidence is the best proof of systematic investigation, the Act does not impose an absolute "repeatability" documentary precondition; where testing occurred on a cast-in-situ concrete forming medium and achieved a patented technological advance (and the lead engineer had died before trial), systematic investigation was reasonably inferred26.
Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 773
Fixed-price commercial contracts vs. contract payments

Held that fixed-price commercial subcontracts to deliver space hardware where the taxpayer bore the financial and technological risk were ordinary commercial revenue, not "contract payments" reducing SR&ED pools under s. 127(9)21.
Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, [1999] 4 C.T.C. 2701
Failed projects & rejection of hypotheses
Held that a project that fails to achieve its objective still achieves a technological advancement because the systematic testing and rejection of a hypothesis advances technological knowledge26.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740
Appellate endorsement of Northwest Hydraulic & software claims

Formally adopted the 5-question Northwest Hydraulic test as the binding appellate standard in Canada; dismissed a custom lottery software claim (IDLS, 1991–1995) due to lack of contemporaneous documentation, failure to call direct developer witnesses, and expert testimony (Dr. Takagaki) showing routine software engineering26.
Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597
Substantiation of SR&ED activities and costs
Emphasized the taxpayer's evidentiary burden to link claimed development activities and expenditures to systematic investigation rather than general commercial development26.
1373744 Ontario Inc. (One Source Metal) v. The Queen, 2009 TCC 511
Missing technical report at the 18-month s. 37(11) deadline

Dismissed a 2005 SR&ED appeal where Form T661 was date-stamped at the CRA office on March 28, 2007 (before the March 31, 2007 deadline), but the file copy of the technical report bore no CRA date stamp and was only faxed on April 12, 2007 (after the 18-month deadline)26.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 (aff'd 2011 FCA 355)
TCC & FCA (2011)
Routine engineering vs. technological uncertainty

Dismissed a 2005 SR&ED claim for overhauling thermoformed plastic "Multi-Bins" despite systematic testing of 8 plastics (PETG, PVC, acrylic, ABS, styrene, Lexan, HDPE, polyethylene) and moulds, holding that testing known resins and standard thermoforming techniques ("plug-assist") accessible to competent professionals is routine engineering, not technological uncertainty26.
Murray Arlin Dentistry PC v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 133
Database tracking & time allocation substantiation

Dismissed a periodontist's 2007–2008 claims ($103,950/yr) for tracking 50 variables across 12,000 dental implant records in commercial software (Tritan); held that automated software tables and uncorroborated estimates of 350 hours/yr failed to prove systematic investigation or substantiate the 20% salary allocation, and rejected "first-time claimant leniency"26.
1726437 Ontario Inc. (Airmax Technologies) v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376
System uncertainty in HVAC integration & Informal Procedure cap

Allowed $387,553 in 2007–2008 SR&ED expenditures where combining a European boiler, Korean Essen Tech ECM motor, air diffusers, and perforated flexible ductwork created genuine system uncertainty in reducing townhouse HVAC noise from 60 dB to 40 dB; however, because the taxpayer elected the Informal Procedure, additional refundable ITC relief for 2008 was capped at $12,00026.
Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58 (aff'd 2015 FCA)
Implied undertaking rule in Tax Court discovery

Held that the CRA breached the common-law implied undertaking rule (Juman v. Doucette) by using 260 documents obtained for the first time during Tax Court pre-trial discovery on April 12, 2012, to issue new reassessments against the taxpayer in October 2012; awarded $25,000 in costs to Fio and barred the CRA from using the discovery documents in any other proceeding without leave26.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313
Manufacturing process improvements, multi-year projects & CRA expert bias

Allowed 4 automated appliance-assembly process projects ($400k salaries, $5k materials in 2009); held that (1) cost-effective manufacturing process improvements can constitute technological advancement, (2) projects must be evaluated holistically across multiple years, (3) credible oral testimony can overcome sparse contemporaneous records (116736 Canada Inc.), and (4) the CRA science adviser who audited the file lacked the independence required of an expert witness26.
6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77
Post-commercial-release SR&ED & system-level evaluation

Allowed 2009 ($103,628) and 2010 ($49,688) ITC claims for a miniature wireless portable printer (1.5" × 1.5" × 10"); held that initial commercial release of 200 units in late 2008 did not preclude subsequent SR&ED claims when over 20% failed due to paper-curling and battery-drain uncertainties arising from extreme system geometry constraints26.
Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 301 (aff'g 2015 TCC 211)
Strict 18-month deadline for Schedule T2SCH31 (ITA s. 127(9)(m))

Held that even though the taxpayer filed Form T661 on time on June 30, 2010, and the CRA accepted $95,791 of 2008 SR&ED expenditures, filing prescribed Schedule T2SCH31 late on August 16, 2010, was fatal to claiming the ITC; Section 32 of the Interpretation Act cannot cure the failure to file Schedule 31 by the 18-month deadline26.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6
Failure to consult qualified engineers & discarding failed designs

Dismissed 2008–2009 mechanical rigging claims (counterweight-free theatre fire curtain descent in ≤30 seconds & $5,000 manual stage curtain override) where the claimant employed no professional engineers, failed to establish that standard engineering could not solve the problem, discarded failed sketches, and relied on after-the-fact "Experiment Summary Sheets" drafted by tax consultants26.
Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 21
Literature reviews without experimental testing or analysis

Dismissed 2012 applied research claims for 3 natural health product formulations (Laetrile, Neuro Support, Cardio Support) where the naturopathic founder conducted literature reviews and paper formulations without performing clinical trials, laboratory experiments, or systematic testing of hypotheses26.
Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 FCA 57 (aff'g 2017 TCC 9)
Leaving Part 2 narrative boxes blank on Form T661 (s. 37(11))

Held that filing Form T661 with the Part 2 technical narrative boxes left blank (arguing the CRA already possessed the information from a related company's accepted claim for the same project) violated subsections 37(11) and 37(12), resulting in complete denial of the claim26.
A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 48
System uncertainty in heavy CNC machine design & abandoned projects

Allowed 2006–2008 SR&ED claims in large part for designing an 80-ton welded-steel horizontal lathe (Project #4) and a double-wheel roll grinding machine with ceramic bearings and linear guideways (Project #6, even though abandoned due to severe vibration), holding that non-trivial integration of components at extreme tolerances created valid system uncertainty (while denying 2006 claims for attempting to repair purchased Italian Tacchi lathes)26.
Béton Mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 278
Accessible professional knowledge vs. technological uncertainty

Allowed 6 of 14 concrete formulation projects; articulated at para. 43 that if a problem can be resolved predictably using techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, there is no technological uncertainty even if the path was initially uncertain to the claimant26.
National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (aff'd 2022 FCA 72)
Self-imposed cost/tool constraints vs. technological uncertainty

Dismissed an SR&ED consulting firm's 2011 claim ($68,029 expenses / $23,810 ITC) for developing a web-based Project Tracking System using legacy ADO, Classic ASP, COM+, and SQL Server 2000; held that obstacles caused by self-imposed financial and skill restrictions (limiting tools to those already owned and known by staff) are not technological uncertainty, and code snippets without revision history fail the record-keeping test52.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246)
Mandatory nature of the "scientific method" criterion

Dismissed appeal for 2009–2010 taxation years; rejected the taxpayer's textual argument that because s. 248(1) does not contain the exact words "scientific method," the 3rd Northwest Hydraulic criterion should not apply, reaffirming that Northwest Hydraulic is the binding purposive interpretation of s. 248(1)26.
CAE Inc. v. His Majesty The King, 2022 FCA 178 (aff'g 2021 TCC 57)
Below-market government R&D loans as "government assistance"

Held that the entire principal of financial contributions/loans received in 2012–2013 under Industry Canada's Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) for "Project Falcon" constituted "government assistance" under s. 127(9) (rejecting CAE's request to separate the capital loan from the below-market interest rate differential), reducing CAE's SR&ED ITCs and increasing taxable income26.
Buehler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18
System uncertainty in heavy agricultural tractor integration
Taxpayer Win: Allowed SR&ED claims for tractor design, providing a strong judicial illustration of how complex subsystem integration issues generate eligible system uncertainty26.
Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 35
Baseline knowledge of a competent professional

Dismissed jewellery manufacturing claims; reinforced Béton Mobile that technological uncertainty must be evaluated against the baseline knowledge of a competent specialist (e.g., B.Sc. in the field of science), not an artisan without scientific training55.
DAZZM Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129
Modern cloud SaaS & open-source framework (React/Redux) integration

Major Software Taxpayer Win: Allowed SR&ED claims for resolving systemic architectural and performance uncertainties when integrating open-source tools (React/Redux) in a cloud-based SaaS platform; confirmed that software projects must be evaluated holistically rather than dismissed as routine debugging26.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 159 (issued Jan 17, 2025)
Food & beverage processing & contemporaneous records

Taxpayer Win: Allowed 2020 SR&ED claim for developing a shelf-stable (2+ years at room temperature) cold-pressed canned juice ("Chrisoda") without pasteurization after initial cans exploded from microbial oxygen release; testing a dairy preservative (Chiber) outside its known domain via measurable pH and microbial observations satisfied all 5 Northwest Hydraulic criteria44.
Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146
Strict 1-year + 90-day statutory bar on late Notices of Objection

Denied application to extend time to object to 2020–2021 assessments mailed September 13, 2022, where the taxpayer objected on January 18, 2024 (past the December 12, 2023 1-year + 90-day limit); held that CRA officer affidavits proving automated BCCS/Print-to-Mail dispatch establish mailing on a balance of probabilities under s. 244(14) and trigger non-rebuttable deemed receipt under s. 248(7)(a)26.
Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173
Plagiarized technical narratives, statute-barred years & s. 163(2) penalties

Split decision allowing legitimate 2007–2008 heating element projects (tubular line, flexible silicone/Kapton, annealed elements) but denying 2006 and 2009 claims; held that copying supplier/website text into SR&ED technical reports was a misrepresentation that reopened statute-barred years and supported s. 163(2) penalties55.
Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7
System uncertainty (allowed) vs. software modernization/scale-up (disallowed)

Landmark 2026 Split Decision: Allowed the MTCLM SIL-4 train-control box project based on cumulative "system uncertainty" not resolvable by available methods, but disallowed $1,293,692 on the SCADACOM-5 project, holding that modernizing and scaling up industrial control software using known tools is product development, not experimental development55.

9.1 Interaction Between Provincial Tax Credits and the Federal SR&ED Pool (The Grind)

Every province in Canada (except Prince Edward Island) and one territory (Yukon) provides a statutory R&D tax credit3. Under subsection 127(9), paragraph 37(1)(d), and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance"3. Consequently, unless a corporation formally renounces (waives) a non-refundable provincial tax credit on or before its federal income tax return filing-due date (6 months after year-end), the provincial tax credit earned for the year reduces both the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 429) and the federal Part 4 qualified SR&ED expenditure pool (Line 513/514) dollar-for-dollar2. Furthermore, because each province legislates its own corporate tax statute, the federal SR&ED expansions enacted in Bill C-15 (the $6,000,000 limit, ECPC access, and restored capital expenditures) do NOT automatically pass through to provincial regimes unless the province amends or harmonizes its provincial statute3.

body.text: 9.2 Deep Dive: Québec's 2025–2026 Overhaul — From Legacy RS&DE Credits to the CRIC and CDAEIA

In the 2025–2026 Québec Budget tabled on March 25, 2025 (and detailed in Québec Finance Information Bulletin 2025-6 and Revenu Québec guidelines updated in July and September 2026), the Government of Québec enacted a comprehensive restructuring of its provincial R&D and innovation tax incentives8.

Effective for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec repealed its legacy R&D salary tax credit (Form RD-1029.7-V), university/public research centre credit (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), private partnership pre-competitive research credit (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), research consortium fees credit (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V—subject to a transitional carryforward rule allowing cumulative consortium fees/dues balances to be claimed for taxation years ending no later than December 31, 2029), technological adaptation services credit, and the tax holidays for foreign researchers and foreign experts, consolidating them into the single Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T8. (For taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025, the legacy credits continue to apply, offering a 30% refundable rate on the first $3,000,000 of eligible expenditures for Canadian-controlled corporations with prior-year assets of $50,000,000 or less—phased out linearly to the 14% base rate for assets between $50,000,000 and $75,000,000—subject to an exclusion threshold scaling linearly from $50,000 at ≤$50,000,000 of assets to $225,000 at ≥$75,000,000 of assets, filed with Form RD-222-V.)14

Under the new CRIC (available to corporations and corporate partners operating a business with an establishment in Québec for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025), Québec expanded eligibility beyond scientific research and experimental development (which remains harmonized with the federal subsection 248(1) definition and is scientifically reviewed by the CRA) to include pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation (reported with Form RD-1029.8.PR-T)3. Eligible pre-commercialization activities comprise: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation; (2) product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials; and (3) quality control activities relating to the implementation of a quality control system required to obtain initial regulatory approval or certification3.

Qualified expenditures for the CRIC include: 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees in Québec; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for an eligible contract carried out in Québec; 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and 100% of property acquisition costs (new depreciable capital property) used directly in Québec for R&D or pre-commercialization (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings, and excluding property claimed under the C3i investment and innovation credit or a large investment project tax holiday)8. Before computing the CRIC, the corporation must subtract an annual applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of: (i) $50,000, or (ii) the sum of the basic personal amount under the Québec personal income tax system ($18,571 in 2025) for each employee, adjusted to reflect the proportion of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities8. Regardless of company size or foreign ownership, the CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold (allocated among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 limit8.

In parallel, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, Québec modernized its Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE) into the CDAEIA, refocusing the 30% IT salary credit (which requires an annual Investissement Québec certificate applied for within 15 months of fiscal year-end) on corporations that meaningfully integrate Artificial Intelligence (AI) functionalities (such as chatbots, virtual assistants, voice recognition, natural language processing, personalized recommendation systems, metadata analysis, and predictive tools), while adding data processing and hosting activities and excluding routine maintenance or scaling89. Across 2024 to 2028+, the total 30% credit shifts between refundable and non-refundable portions: 24% refundable + 6% non-refundable in 2024; 23% + 7% in 2025; 22% + 8% in 2026; 21% + 9% in 2027; and 20% + 10% in 2028 and subsequent years (and is halved to 15% total—11% + 4% in 2026, 10.5% + 4.5% in 2027, and 10% + 5% in 2028+—when at least 50% of gross revenue is derived from an application developed for exclusive use outside Québec by a related entity)89.
10. Direct Federal R&D Grants, Stacking Mechanics, and Intellectual Property Policy
10.1 National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)

Operating alongside the retrospective SR&ED tax credit is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), Canada's premier direct, non-repayable R&D contribution program for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)5. According to industry advisory analyses of NRC IRAP program data for the 2024–2025 fiscal year, IRAP provided $393.1 million in contributions to 3,136 companies, advised more than 9,187 firms, and supported an estimated 23,208 jobs5.

To be eligible for NRC IRAP funding, an applicant must be an incorporated, for-profit company operating in Canada with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) employees, pursue a technology-driven mandate to develop and commercialize innovative products, services, or processes involving technical uncertainty, be financially stable to cover its unassisted cost share, and be in good standing with the CRA5. Foreign-owned Canadian subsidiaries with ≤500 FTEs are eligible if the R&D is performed in Canada and generates economic benefits in Canada, whereas sole proprietorships, partnerships, cooperatives, ULCs/LLCs, and non-profits are ineligible for direct funding5. Unlike SR&ED, IRAP is an advisor-driven program delivered through a network of Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) that requires project approval before costs are incurred5. Under IRAP's 80/50 cost-sharing model, non-repayable contributions reimburse up to 80% of eligible internal technical salaries and up to 50% of eligible subcontractor costs5. IRAP operates across four streams: (1) Core IRAP (with tiered decision service standards of 20 business days for contributions ≤$50,000; 30 business days for $50,000–$500,000; 45 business days for $500,000–$3,000,000; and 65 business days for $3,000,000–$10,000,000); (2) Large Value Contributions (up to $10,000,000 per firm, which directed $76,000,000 to 72 SMEs in 2024–2025); (3) AI Assist (a $100,000,000 AI innovation program); and (4) Defence Industrial Strategy programs, alongside 40 to 60 hours of no-cost Management Advisory Services (MAS) delivered in partnership with CMC-Canada5.
10.2 Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) and Canadian Patent Box Policy Status

Established in 2017 and administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) allocates large-scale repayable and non-repayable contributions (for multi-year projects exceeding 36 months with contributions of $10,000,000 or more) to firms of all sizes across five streams: Streams 1 to 3 (Business Innovation and Growth: R&D commercialization, firm growth/expansion, and large-scale investment attraction) and Streams 4 and 5 (Collaborations and Networks: industrial R&D consortia and national innovation ecosystems, alongside clean-growth and GHG reduction commitments)105. As established in CAE Inc. v. His Majesty The King, 2022 FCA 178, both non-repayable grants and repayable below-market government contributions under programs such as SIF or SADI constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, reducing the recipient's federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar in the year received/receivable (and only generating SR&ED ITCs in subsequent years as repayments are actually made on Line 560)20.

Regarding intellectual property (IP) income taxation, although the federal Department of Finance conducted consultations in 2024 and indicated in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement an intention to propose a federal patent box regime, no federal patent box proposal was included in the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget or Bill C-1510. Consequently, as of November 2026, Canada has no enacted federal patent box regime38.
10.3 Comprehensive Mathematical Stacking Model: Federal SR&ED + Provincial Credit + NRC IRAP

Because government assistance (including NRC IRAP contributions and provincial R&D tax credits) reduces federal SR&ED qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar under subsection 127(18), however the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4) is computed on the unreduced gross SR&ED salary base (Part 5, Line 818) before government assistance is deducted in Part 4 (Lines 513–517), stacking NRC IRAP with SR&ED and provincial credits preserves the full 55% proxy overhead notional base5.
